document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners in response to certain parties’ protests and comments on PJM Interconnection,…

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.   
 
)  
 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF  
THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“Commission”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213, the Indicated PJM 
Transmission Owners1 submit this Answer in response to certain parties’ protests and comments 
on PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) 60-Day Compliance Filing in the above-captioned 
proceeding.2 
 
1  
For purposes of this filing, the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners are: American Electric Power Service 
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky 
Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP Appalachian 
Transmission Company, AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, AEP Kentucky Transmission Company, 
AEP Ohio Transmission Company, and AEP West Virginia Transmission Company; The Dayton Power and Light 
Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a 
Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business Services, LLC for Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy 
Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its 
affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, 
Commonwealth Edison Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and 
Potomac Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates American Transmission 
Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The 
Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company, Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, and 
Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities 
Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas Company; Rockland Electric Company; and the Southern Maryland 
Electric Cooperative (“PJM Transmission Owners”). 
2  
To the extent required, the PJM Transmission Owners respectfully move for leave to answer.  The 
Commission’s procedural rules generally prohibit answers to protests.  Specifically, Rule 213 states that “[a]n answer 
may not be made to a protest . . . unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.”  18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).  
The Commission has the discretion to waive its prohibition of answers to protests for good cause shown, i.e., to assist 
the Commission’s understanding and resolution of the issues raised or to ensure a complete record.  See, e.g., Pioneer 
Transmission, LLC v. N. Ind. Pub. Serv. Co., 140 FERC ¶ 61,057, at P 94 (2012); Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. 
Operator, Inc., 120 FERC ¶ 61,083, at P 23 (2007); Morgan Stanley Cap. Grp., Inc. v. N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 
93 FERC ¶ 61,017, at 61,036 (2000); CNG Transmission Corp., 89 FERC ¶ 61,100, at 61,287 n.11 (1999).  This 
Answer is submitted to ensure a complete and accurate record.  Accordingly, good cause exists to permit this answer.

2 
I. 
ANSWER TO PROTESTS AND COMMENTS 
A. 
Behind-the-Meter Generation 
In its 60-Day Compliance Filing, PJM proposes revisions to the Behind the Meter 
Generation (“BTMG”) provisions in its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to comply 
with the Commission’s December 18, 2025 Order, which directed PJM to propose a new 
materiality threshold for Retail BTMG, establish a three-year transition period, and provide legacy 
treatment for certain existing contractual arrangements above the new threshold.3 
PJM proposes to establish a materiality threshold of up to 50 MW for Retail BTMG 
eligibility based on the cumulative nameplate rating of generation used to serve retail load by a 
Network Customer4 at the at the same electrical location, excluding qualifying backup generation, 
while otherwise preserving existing substantive netting rules.5  Several commenters argue that a 
nameplate-based threshold is inappropriate and urge the Commission to adopt a materially higher 
threshold, such as 200 MW.6   
The Commission should reject those arguments because the 50 MW threshold strikes the 
appropriate balance between allowing continued use of Retail BTMG and appropriate limitations 
to ensure reliability.  The Order expressly directed PJM to propose a new MW threshold for Retail 
BTMG and explained that such a threshold should reduce the reliability and resource adequacy 
 
3  
See PJM 60-Day Compliance Filing, Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 4 (filed Feb. 23, 2026); see also PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at PP 179, 221-224 (2025) (“Order”). 
4  
Terms not otherwise defined herein shall have the same meaning as set forth in the PJM Tariff. 
5  
PJM 60-Day Compliance Filing at 5-17. 
6  
See Protest of Calibrant Energy; Antora Energy, Inc.; Convergent Energy and Power; Eolian L.P.; and 
Mainspring Energy, Inc., Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 6-8, 11-12 (filed Mar. 16, 2026) (collectively, the “BTMG 
Parties”); Comments of Crusoe Technologies LLC, Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 2, 4-5 (filed Mar. 16, 2026) 
(“Crusoe”); Joint Protest and Comments of the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition, the Industrial Energy Consumers 
of America, and the National Railroad Passenger Corporation, Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 5, 9, 23-33 (filed Mar. 
16, 2026); Protest and Comments of Eastman Chemical Company, Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 6 (filed Mar. 16, 
2026).

3 
risks posed by large Retail BTMG, while allowing smaller customers to continue netting in a 
transparent and not unduly discriminatory manner.7  PJM reasonably selected 50 MW because that 
threshold aligns with the PJM Board’s definition of large load additions, preserves existing 
treatment for smaller and longstanding Retail BTMG arrangements, and avoids sweeping in retail 
customers whose grid impacts are comparatively limited.8  PJM reasonably based the threshold on 
generator size—measured by cumulative nameplate rating—because generator capacity is static 
and administrable, whereas load can fluctuate.9  The Commission should therefore reject 
commenters’ requests to materially increase the MW threshold or replace PJM’s brightline, 
nameplate-based standard with a more variable approach. 
However, it is important that this threshold be paired with grandfathering provisions that 
appropriately recognize that industrial and commercial customers have relied on Retail BTMG 
rules and that eliminating the ability to continue relying on those provisions could cause them 
substantial financial harm.  To that end, the PJM Transmission Owners support certain proposed 
additions and clarifications to PJM’s grandfathering proposal, namely: 
 Grandfathering treatment should extend to projects that are not yet in service and would 
have been eligible for Retail BTMG treatment, but have made substantial progress 
towards completion. 
 The “existing contract” exception to the application of the new Retail BTMG rules 
should be construed broadly to cover a wide range of contracts and recognition of 
renewal rights in those contracts. 
 
7  
Order at PP 186, 221. 
8  
PJM 60-Day Compliance Filing at 11-13. 
9  
Id. at 14.

4 
 Grandfathering treatment should be extended to existing Retail BTMG arrangements 
that have been physically in service and operating for a significant period of time to 
avoid disrupting these long-standing arrangements. 
B. 
Transmission Services for Co-Located Load 
Consistent with the Order, PJM proposes Tariff revisions establishing the transmission-
service framework applicable to Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-
Located Load, including three new transmission service options in addition to Network Integration 
Transmission Service (“NITS”).10   
1. 
The Commission Should not Mandate a Combined Interconnection 
and Transmission Study Process for Co-Located Loads and Generation 
In its comments, Invenergy Renewables LLC and Invenergy Thermal LLC argue that the 
Commission and PJM should clarify how the transmission and generator interconnection study 
processes can work in tandem.11  In Invenergy’s view, developers and lenders will be reluctant to 
commit to projects without both sets of study results showing that the project is viable and 
identifying expected upgrade costs, and coordinated studies would better align generation and 
load, improve efficiency, reduce system costs, and provide the certainty needed for co-location 
projects to be financed and developed at scale.12 
Invenergy’s comments primarily address PJM’s initial brief in the paper hearing process 
imposed by the Commission in Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al.,13 and the PJM Transmission Owners 
will respond fully to those comments in that proceeding.  However, because Invenergy also 
 
10  
PJM 60-Day Compliance Filing at 18. 
11  
Comments of Invenergy Renewables LLC and Invenergy Thermal LLC, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al., at 5 
(filed Mar. 16, 2026) (“Invenergy”). 
12  
Id. at 4. 
13  
Order at PP 2, 219-220.

5 
included the PJM 60-Day Compliance Filing docket in the caption of its comments, the PJM 
Transmission Owners summarize their response here as well.   
It is unclear what Invenergy is asking for here, but to the extent it is requesting that the 
Commission impose a combined transmission and interconnection study process for Co-Located 
Load and generation, the Commission should decline.  In its initial brief in the paper hearing 
process, PJM has already proposed a coordinated load and generation study process, with the PJM 
Transmission Owners conducting load integration studies and PJM performing generator 
interconnection and transmission service studies, as necessary.  Requiring PJM to administer a 
single study process goes beyond the issues set for hearing by the Commission in the Order, as 
well as the scope of compliance directed by the Commission in the instant proceeding.   
Finally, end-use load is still retail load and existing load interconnection rules set forth in 
state jurisdictional tariffs and agreements cannot be ignored or sidestepped.  However, there is no 
need for the Commission to entangle itself in questions regarding the division between its 
jurisdiction over interstate transmission matters and state jurisdiction over retail service in this 
proceeding.  The coordinated study approach proposed by PJM will provide a just and reasonable 
opportunity for Co-Located Load to interconnect and assess the appropriate type and level of 
transmission service that it wishes to obtain. 
2. 
Use of New Transmission Services by Behind-the-Meter Generation 
and Load-Only Customers 
The Joint Parties14  ask the Commission to reject, or at least defer action on, PJM’s proposal 
to limit PJM’s new transmission service options to Co-Located Load, while excluding Retail 
BTMG customers and other load-only customers that can limit withdrawals from the grid unless 
 
14  
Protest of Eolian L.P.; Antora Energy, Inc.; Calibrant Energy; Convergent Energy and Power; Mainspring 
Energy, Inc.; and Verrus, LLC, Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 10-15 (filed Mar. 16, 2026) (collectively, the “Joint 
Parties”).

6 
PJM revises the tariff to make the new transmission services available to BTMG and similarly 
situated load-only customers.15  According to the Joint Parties, BTMG-served loads and similarly 
flexible load-only customers are sufficiently comparable to Co-Located Load that they should have 
access to the same transmission service options, rather than being required to take full NITS simply 
because they are not connected to a generating facility with PJM interconnection rights.16 
The Commission should reject the Joint Parties’ request that it reject or defer action on 
PJM’s proposal to limit the new transmission service options to Co-Located Load.  In the Order, 
the Commission made clear that the new transmission services are limited to Eligible Customers 
taking transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Load, and repeatedly described NITS, Firm 
Contract Demand Transmission Service, and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service 
as options available only within that Co-Located Load framework.17   
While a number of PJM Transmission Owners disagree that the new transmission services 
are necessary at all, there is absolutely no evidence in the record to suggest that load-only 
customers should be entitled to utilize these transmission services.  Those customers must continue 
to take NITS.  Moreover, the Joint Parties’ assertion that Co-Located Load and ordinary BTMG 
or other load-only customers are “similarly situated” should be rejected because it ignores the line 
the Commission expressly drew in the Order.  The Commission did not establish a generally 
available transmission-service option for any customer that claims it can limit withdrawals from 
the grid.  Rather, it directed PJM to create those new services only for an Eligible Customer taking 
transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Load, which the Commission defined as load 
 
15  
Joint Parties at 10-12, 14-15. 
16  
Id. at 10-14. 
17

7 
physically connected to an Interconnection Customer’s existing or planned generator.18  The new 
services are tied to generator-specific attributes that ordinary load-only customers do not share, 
including an associated generator, separate metering from that generator, and the ability and 
willingness to prevent or limit withdrawals through the co-location configuration itself.19  The 
Commission also declined to comprehensively address retail load interconnection more generally, 
confirming that the replacement rate was directed to Co-Located Load, not load-only customers as 
a class.20 
3. 
Permitting Interim NITS Customers to Serve On-Site Load with On-
Site Generation During a Curtailment 
The Data Center Coalition and Crusoe argue that PJM’s proposed Interim NITS framework 
is unworkable unless a curtailed customer may continue to serve on-site load with co-located 
generation.21  They contend that curtailment should limit withdrawals from the transmission 
system, not prevent a customer from using its own co-located generation or Retail BTMG, because 
otherwise Interim NITS would provide little or no practical value and significantly undermine the 
viability of co-location arrangements.22  They therefore urge the Commission to clarify that an 
Interim NITS customer may continue to use co-located generator during curtailment, including 
while the generator remains in the interconnection study process.23 
The PJM Transmission Owners do not oppose the requested clarification that Interim NITS 
customers be permitted to continue serving on-site load with co-located generation during a

curtailment event, provided that PJM implements appropriate safeguards to ensure that any such 
operation does not result in unreserved use of the transmission system or otherwise compromise 
reliability.  This position is consistent with the Commission’s recognition in the Order that, when 
curtailed, an Eligible Customer taking Interim NITS on behalf of Co-Located Load “may be able 
to continue to take energy from the Interconnection Customer with which they are co-located if 
PJM’s Tariff otherwise allows.”24 
II. 
CONCLUSION 
The PJM Transmission Owners respectfully request that the Commission accept this 
answer and that any subsequent Commission orders addressing these issues be consistent with the 
discussion herein. 
 
Respectfully submitted,
